Summary
In this chapter, you learned about object orientation, a concept that is exhibited
throughout the rest of the book. Because of its structure of GameObjects with
components, Unity is perfectly designed for an OOP mindset. You also learned about
component-oriented design, a programming design pattern that works very well with
Unity and—while a bit more complicated to implement—can make your code simpler
and more manageable.
Along with the idea of component-oriented OOP comes the concept of modularity. In
many ways, modular code is the opposite of monolithic code. Modular coding focuses
on making small, reusable functions and classes that do one thing really well. Because
modular classes and functions are small (usually fewer than 500 lines), they are easier to
debug and understand. Modular code is also designed to be reusable.
In the following chapter, you'll learn about data-oriented design and Unity's new Data-
Oriented Tech Stack (DOTS). DOTS encompasses several new technologies that Unity is
moving toward, which have the potential to drastically increase the performance of our
Unity games but require a very different mindset than OOP (and as of Unity 2020.3 are
not yet fully implemented).
After that, you'll start Part III of the book, a series of focused tutorials that will help you
learn how to start prototypes for various kinds of games. I hope you enjoy what you find
there and can use them to start your journey as a designer, prototyper, and developer.

58124.content:
DATA-ORIENTED DESIGN
While object-oriented programming has been
the dominant form of programming taught
over the past four decades, it may surprise you
to learn that object-oriented code doesn't work
at all well with modern memory architecture
or multi-threaded computer processors. The
alternative is data-oriented design. While not
necessary in most projects, when needed,
Unity's Data-Oriented Tech Stack can cause
code execution speed to increase by up to one
thousand times!
In this chapter you will learn about DOTS
and get a glimpse of the possible future
of programming, along with a DOTS code
tutorial.

The Theory of Data-Oriented Design
Data-Oriented Design (DOD) is not new, but it has seen a resurgence over the last two
decades, driven especially by the limitations of console hardware and the ways in which
processors and graphics cards have improved recently. The core concept of DOD is that
all programming is data manipulation,
1
and efficient programming is code that considers
how that data is actually used and transferred by the processor.
Realities of Modern Computer Hardware
There are several technological considerations that are addressed by Data-Oriented
Design:
2
The Limitations of Moore's Law
In 1965, Gordon Moore, the co-founder of Fairchild Semiconductor and eventual CEO
of Intel, predicted a yearly doubling of transistors in integrated circuits for at least a
decade. In 1975, he revised this to a doubling every two years. This prediction held true
so consistently that it became known as "Moore's Law." Every two years or so, the perfor-
mance of a central processing unit (CPU), the main processor of a computer, doubled as
individual transistors got smaller and smaller—until it became extremely difficult to make
them any smaller (to the point that individual wires on chips are only a couple atoms
thick!). Starting in 2010, this had a profound effect on processor speed and design.
As you can see in the chart in Figure 28.1 by Karl Rupp, though the number of transis-
tors continues to increase, single-thread performance and clock speed (i.e., frequency
[MHz]) have stopped increasing. However, the number of logical cores started increas-
ing exponentially in about 2005, which brings us to…
Increasing Numbers of Processor Cores
Now, nearly all processors in computers, game consoles, and mobile devices are multi-
core, meaning that rather than a single ridiculously large processor, they instead have
a CPU containing several smaller processors that work in parallel. However, computer
code for parallel processing is notoriously difficult to write. So even now, even though
my computer's processor has eight cores, most code in Unity still executes in a single

Data Locality and Access Speed
While your processor—any processor you own—is objectively very fast, it doesn't mat-
ter how fast it is if it doesn't have the data it needs at hand. All processors can only act
on the data in their registers, and the further the data is from that register, the more
time it will take for the computer to access it. A computer has several different levels of
data access, and each subsequent level holds more data but takes significantly longer
to access. In 2010, Dr. Jeff Dean (current lead of Google AI) gave a somewhat famous
talk
4
at Stanford University, in which he described several things they learned over the
previous decade at Google. The salient one for us here is his "Numbers Everyone Should
Know," which described access times at various levels of the computer. You can see an
updated (and simplified) version of this in Figure 28.2.

Although the times to access data on hard disks are insanely large, the most common

Cache, 25 times slower than L2 cache, and 100 times slower than L1 Cache. So, the
major goal of data-oriented design is to make sure that the data your processor needs is
in the caches rather than in RAM.

a time, which is referred to as a cache line (equivalent to sixteen 32-bit integers (or floats),
eight 4-byte RGBA colors, or about five 3-float positions). Because of cache lines, if all the
data you need is located close to each other in RAM, you get something called a cache
hit, when the processor can act on the next piece of data without having to resort to
pulling the data from RAM. Additionally, modern processors will attempt to predict what
RAM data they will need next and prefetch that data from RAM into a cache. So if large
amounts of data are organized well, the computer can correctly predict what it needs to
pull into caches and greatly increase performance. If your data is organized well, that is
good data locality. On the other hand, bad data locality leads to frequent cache misses.
The Issues with Object-Oriented Programming
Now that you know a bit about the internals of how the processor and memory of
your computer, tablet, or mobile phone work, we can take a look at what's wrong with
object-oriented programming. More than anything else, it comes down to data locality
and the programmer's lack of ability to manage data locality in OOP.

Unity's Data-Oriented Tech Stack
Data-oriented design focuses first and foremost on data locality: getting the right data in
the right place for the processor to handle it efficiently. By organizing data efficiently and
managing access to that data, Unity's Data-Oriented Tech Stack (DOTS
8
) solves most
of the data issues present in Unity's traditional OOP approach. Unity DOTS comprises
three core technologies that collaborate to provide what Unity calls "performance by
default"; that is, code that is performant due to its structure without requiring addi-
tional optimization. The three technologies are:
9
■ C# Job System: A highly optimized code library that allows developers to write safe
multithreaded code.
■ Burst Compiler: By limiting certain "high level" aspects of the C# language, Unity
is able to compile C# code into assembly language that runs faster than C++ code on
the same processor.
■ Entity Component System (ECS): A new paradigm for code organization based
entirely on data-oriented design. Unity ECS also includes the tools to convert Unity
GameObjects to this new paradigm.
Unfortunately, at this time, Unity ECS is still incomplete. Throughout most of the months
that I was writing the third edition of this book, Unity ECS changed so frequently that

you build a WebGL project in Unity, the build comprises all of your code and assets on top of
a JavaScript/WebGL library that contains almost all of Unity's functionality. Because so much is
built into it, you end up with pretty large WebGL builds (usually at least 20MB in size). Project
Tiny is a DOTS-based WebGL approach that includes only what is needed. In demos, Unity has
created a full match-three style game, complete with art, that is compressed to a single 70kB
html file (as opposed to the current index.html file that loads assets from a large Build folder).
This is incredibly cool and I believe it will completely revolutionize advergaming (i.e., small
web and mobile games used as advertisements in place of images or videos), but it's not
really relevant to this chapter.

The idea of octaves is to layer different frequencies of noise over each other, thereby
creating a more interesting and varied image. Traditionally, noise octaves have three
primary values:
■ Number of Octaves: How many layers of noise should we combine? Our previous
code is equivalent to a single octave (i.e., only one layer of noise), and the new code
will increase this to 4 octaves (by default).
■ Lacunarity: For each additional octave, how much should the frequency increase?
This is similar to zooming out on our map. Higher frequencies mean more variation,
so a lacunarity of 2 will double the frequency of the noise on each layer, leading to
more and more detail for each octave added.

Avoiding Reference-Based Data
One of the major ways that Unity DOTS improves performance is by restricting the use
of any reference-based data. As discussed earlier, all classes are stored by reference, so
as a result, no classes can be used in DOTS! Instead, DOTS uses structs.
15
A struct is simi-
lar to a class, but it includes no inheritance or polymorphism, and as a result, all the data
in a struct can be stored together in memory, in the same place, as long as each field in

the easiest way I have found to think about it is that data is blittable if it can be stored
as one chunk in the same place.
16
So, it makes sense that a struct composed of only blit-
table data is also blittable itself.
Because classic Unity C# is almost entirely composed of classes, and classes are not
blittable, very little of classic Unity C# can be part of blittable types. As a result, Unity
wrote many new libraries that can replace the Unity classes that we're used to. The clas-

Here, we create a single instance of the PerlinIPage-ob struct. Then, on the

The first thing you noticed was probably not that the new cnoise() method doesn't
have the symmetry issue that the OOP Perlin1oise() method had, though that fix
is pretty cool. You probably first noticed that this is only running at 3 frames per
second! So, then why did we do all that work?!? Give me a minute, and you'll see.
The Burst Compiler Saves the Day!
Now, it's time to see how the Burst Compiler helps the Job System.
1. Open Perlin_DOTS in Visual Studio and add a single line above the PerlinIPage-ob
definition, as shown in Code Listing 28.7.
Code Listing 28.7 Perlin_dots.cs

This >Burst&oPpile@ attribute tells the Burst Compiler to work its magic on all
instances of the PerlinIPage-ob struct.
2. Save the Perlin_DOTS script in Visual Studio, return to Unity, and click Play.
Now that's more like it! On my laptop, just enabling Burst Compile on the PerlinIPage
-ob struct increased speed from less than 3fps to 60fps. That's 20 times faster with
a single line of code, and it shows the power of the Burst Compiler. This is also more
than 6 times faster than the OOP version was before we added octaves (as shown in
Figure 28.7). (If you don't see this speed increase, from the main Unity menu bar, choose
Jobs > Burst and ensure that Enable Compilation is checked.)
Unity put a tremendous amount of time into the Burst Compiler and making it work this
kind of magic. The short version is that regular C# has some specific features that make
it easy to write code but very difficult to compile that code efficiently. The Burst Com-
piler prevents us from using those specific features, which allows it to compile extremely
efficient code. Through testing, Unity has found that machine language compiled by
the Burst Compiler is faster and more efficient than comparable machine language
compiled from C++.

We're going to take the grayscale noise that we have and convert it into what will look

Through use of the C# Job System and Burst Compiler, we were able to create a more
complex version of our procedural image generation that ran at considerably higher
speeds, but there's one major pillar of Unity DOTS that we haven't talked about yet.
Entity Component Systems (ECS)
I didn't cover ECS in the tutorial because as I write this book, Unity's version is still in the
Preview state, and it's changing very frequently. I wrote several ECS examples over the
course of authoring this edition, and every one that I made would no longer compile
just a few months after I wrote it because Unity ECS had changed so much. However,
the theory of ECS is stable, and that is what I'll describe here.
Outside of Unity's implementation, ECS comprises three core concepts:
■ Entities: Conceptually, these are similar to GameObjects, but the actual Entity is just
a single unsigned int that groups a collection of Components.

■ Components: Molecular chunks of data, generally as small as possible.
26
■ Systems: Functions that act on Entities that have the right set of Components. Also
as small as possible to keep coding simple.
Transitioning to an ECS Mindset
In traditional Unity development and OOP, we've been encouraged to think of each
element in our game as an object—represented by a class—with both data and function-
ality. Let's look at how this would work for the classic Atari game Asteroids, which was
designed by Lyle Rains and Ed Logg.
27
Figure 28.15 shows various objects in Asteroids
along with some of the data and functionality they require. For example, in OOP, the
PlayerShip object has a position and Yelocity as well as an 8pdatePosition()
method that moves it each frame.
However, looking at this, you'll see that there are many similarities, as shown in
Figure 28.16.
26. An example of a molecular chunk of data would be something like a position (three floats) or
a quaternion (four floats). By molecular, I mean that it's the smallest chunk of data that you
would need at the same time.
27. For information about Asteroids, see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asteroids_(video_game) —
accessed August 10, 2021. You can also find online versions to play by searching "play aster-
oids" online.

Figure 28.16 Objects in Asteroids share many of the same data types and methods

In object-oriented programming, you could make a MoYing2bMect() class that
included position, velocity, rotation, and collisionRadius (plus the shared methods
8pdatePosition(), Screen:rap(), &ollide(), and Destroy() ) and then make
subclasses for each of the object types, but ECS approaches handling these similarities
differently, as shown in Figure 28.17.
Figure 28.17 Entities, Components, and Systems in Asteroids with shading by ECS Component type
(Note that while Systems exclusively contain functionality, they are not listed with () because each
System is a struct, not a function.)
Components Are Molecules of Data
In ECS, the objects in the game are broken down into Components, which I like to think
of as "molecular" chunks of data—they're not the smallest possible bits (i.e., not atomic);
rather, they're the smallest chunk that you would always need to group. For example,
a 2D position will always need float values for x and y, so storing them together as a
float makes sense. So, you could create a &oPBPosition Component as shown in
Code Listing 28.12. (Note: Code Listing 28.12 is pseudocode, meaning that it gets the

As you can see, it's very small. And every ECS Component you define should be very
small. As molecular data, Components are the smallest chunk of data that you would
always need to access at the same time. Our new &oPBPosition Component will be
used by all sorts of Systems: SysB8pdatePostion, SysBScreen:rap, SysB&ollide,
SysBSpaZnPlayerShot, and SysBSpaZnSPaller$steroids will all read and/or write
&oPBPosition Components.
28
Systems Act on Groups of Components
In ECS, Systems are not associated with specific Entities or types of Entities at all. Instead
every System is designed to act on any and every Entity that has the Components it's
looking for. For example, SysB8pdatePosition will act on any Entity that has both
&oPBPosition and &oPB9elocity Components (see Code Listing 28.13).

4 {

6 }
7 }
8 }
All systems are subclasses of &oPponentSysteP and must override the 2n8pdate()
method, which is called every frame. The code on the third line means: for each Entity
that has both &oPBPosition and &oPB9elocity Components, execute the code on

29
It's also worth noting that the &oPB9elocity Component reference is marked

can schedule several jobs to run in parallel that read from it.
28. If you do wish to associate a System with a specific Entity type (e.g., to add player input to
the PlayerShip Entity), the common practice now is to create an empty &oPBPlayerShip
Component that is only attached to the PlayerShip Entity and then write a System
SysBPlayerInput that only operates on Entities with the &oPBPlayerShip Component.

ECS Storage Minimizes Cache Misses
As shown in Figure 28.18, the Components of all Entities are stored together in arrays of
each Component type. This greatly improves data locality. The example SysB8pdate

Figure 28.18 ECS storage of Components in arrays increases efficiency. 30
An Entity Is an Index
With data organized by Component, the best way to think of an Entity is as an index
that tells you which &oPBPosition, &oPB9elocity, &oPBRotation, and other Compo-
nents in the various arrays all belong together in each Entity.
Because an Entity is a simple index used to find the right Components (as opposed to
a class, which contains memory references to its data), SysB8pdatePosition never
requests any data other than the two Components it needs; none of the other Compo-
nents that are part of each Entity are ever pulled from RAM into cache memory.
The Benefits of ECS
"Performance by default" is Unity's tagline for DOTS, and it is well-earned. The core
structure of ECS ensures that your code is set up very well for data locality, the C# Job
System, and the Burst Compiler, all of which maximize speed and efficiency on mod-
ern processors. Additionally, developers with experience in ECS state that though the
initial transition to ECS was painful, after it was implemented, both the addition of new
features and the debugging of existing features were drastically simpler.
30. The &oPBE[pireTiPe and &oPB$steroidSi]e Component arrays in the right side of

the FUtUre oF UnIty dots 617
The Future of Unity DOTS
Though Unity has committed to DOTS for a few years now, their attitude about it seems
to have shifted. Initially, the messaging was along the lines of "You'll never use OOP
again!" —which was pretty frightening to a lot of people who had spent years learn-
ing both object-oriented programming and the subtleties of how to code for Unity C#.
Lately, this has transitioned to "You should use DOTS when you need it," and "If you
design for DOTS from the beginning, your project will be more performant and simpler
to maintain."
Unity has also begun replacing some of its core code libraries with DOTS versions,
including a Unity Physics system (developed with Havok to replace the older NVIDIA
PhysX system) and new networking code. The Unity Physics system
31
is already working
quite well and incorporates several very cool enhancements, like allowing you to run
multiple physics simulations simultaneously and allowing you to run predictive physics
(e.g., showing the player where all the balls on a pool table will go). The DOTS-based

58152.heading: SET UP THE UNITY DOTS EXAMPLE PROJECT
58152.content:
NetCode networking library is still quite far from release, though some impressive
demos have been created with it.
As I mentioned earlier in the chapter, Unity's ECS library has changed drastically and
rapidly throughout its development. The largest reason for this seems to be that Unity
is working very hard to make ECS code less daunting. So, rather than expecting devel-
opers to create Entities, Components, and Systems from scratch, Unity has created a
conversion workflow that allows developers to create GameObjects in Unity like normal,
which are then converted automatically into Entities at runtime. Beyond explicit conver-
sions, I expect Unity to continue to transition under-the-hood code to DOTS, granting
all developers some benefits of DOTS while still supporting more traditional Unity
development workflows and coding.
To learn more about Unity's strategy around DOTS, I recommend checking out the
Unity DOTS website at https://unity.com/dots .
Unity also gave an excellent series of DOTS talks at Unite Copenhagen 2019, which you
can find by searching for "Unite Copenhagen 2019 DOTS" on YouTube.com. In particu-
lar, Mike Geig does an excellent job of making the case for DOTS in his talk "Converting
Your Game to DOTS."
32
31. See https://unity.com/unity/physics — accessed August 11, 2021.
32. On YouTube at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BNMrevfB6Q0 — accessed August 11,
2021.

Summary
In this chapter, you've glimpsed a bit of the future and gotten a chance to explore a
bit of DOTS code and concepts. There is much more to be learned, and by the time
you read this, DOTS and the resources about it will be better than they are as I write it.
However, if this chapter was daunting to you, it's important to keep in mind that you
can write an excellent game without worrying about DOTS at all, and millions of people
around the world are using Unity to do just that!
The next part of the book will take you through several tutorials to help you learn how
to make various kinds of games and take advantage of various features of Unity. All of
those tutorials are built using object-oriented programming because doing so is still the
best way to learn Unity and start prototyping your game ideas as quickly as possible.
After you've gained more experience with Unity development, I recommend exploring
DOTS further and seeing how it can improve the performance of your games.

622 CHAPTER 29 APPLE PICKER
What You Will Learn
As the first in our series of tutorials, you'll learn several new concepts and review
some from Part II of the book, including:
■ Moving a GameObject to follow the mouse
■ Using InYoNe() to call a function after a specified delay
■ Time-based movement of GameObjects
■ Randomizing the movement of GameObjects
■ Displaying score and high score on screen
■ Using PlayerPrefs to track high score across multiple games
■ Using Physics Layers to specify which GameObjects will collide with others
■ and much more!
Figure 29.1 The finished Apple Picker prototype
The Apple Picker Prototype
In this chapter, you'll make Apple Picker, which you can see in Figure 29.1. It's the
simple game that we outlined in Chapter 16, "Thinking in Digital Systems." If
you didn't read that chapter, it might be worthwhile to go back and check out
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
the PUrPose oF a dIGItal PrototyPe 623
the chapter's "Game Analysis: Apple Picker " section, where I went over flow-
charts of how each object in the game needs to act.
Apple Picker is based on the classic Atari game Kaboom!. In the game, an AppleTree
moves back and forth dropping Apples that players attempt to catch with three Baskets.
Each Apple that is caught by the player is worth 100 points. If the player misses one
Apple, then all Apples on screen disappear, the player loses one Basket, and the game
continues. When all three Baskets have been lost, the game is over.
The Purpose of a Digital Prototype
Before we start making the prototype of Apple Picker, now's probably a good time to
think again about the purpose of a digital prototype. The first part of the book provided
considerable discussion of paper prototypes and why they are useful. Paper game
prototypes help you do the following:
■ Test, reject, and/or refine game mechanics and rules quickly
■ Explore the dynamic behavior of your game and understand the emergent
possibilities created by the rules
■ Ascertain whether rules and gameplay elements are easily understood by players
■ Understand the emotional response that players have to your game
One critical thing that a paper prototype can't do is allow you—and playtesters—to see
how the game feels. This is the primary purpose of a digital prototype. Although you
could spend hours describing game mechanics to someone in detail, having them just
play the game and see how it feels is much more efficient (and more interesting). This is
discussed at length in the book Game Feel by Steve Swink.
1
In this chapter, you create a working game, and the end result will be something that
you can show to friends and colleagues. After letting them play it for a while, you can ask
whether the difficulty feels too easy, too difficult, or just right. Use that information to

SET UP THE PROJECT FOR THIS CHAPTER
Follow the standard project setup procedure outlined in Appendix A, "Standard
Project Setup Procedure," to create a new project in Unity. If you need a refresher
on the standard project setup procedure, see Appendix A.
■ Project Template: 3D Core
■ Project Name: Apple Picker
■ Scene Name: _Scene_0
■ Game Pane Dimensions: (you'll set these in the chapter)
You don't need to create any scripts at the beginning of this project, but you
should rename the default Sample Scene to _Scene_0 and follow the instructions
to set up the Game Pane, WebGL build, and Unity version control for this project.
It could save you a ton of time if anything goes wrong. Also make sure to choose
the IGDPD Layout for your Unity window.
Preparing
Happily, you already did a lot of the preparation for this prototype in Chapter 16,
"Thinking in Digital Systems," when we analyzed Apple Picker and the classic game
Kaboom!. As mentioned in that chapter, Apple Picker will have the same basic game
mechanics as Kaboom!. Understanding classic games and how they work is very useful
for you as a designer, and this is a nice easy game to start with.
Take a moment to look back at Chapter 16 and make sure that you understand the flow
charts for each element: the AppleTree, the Apple, and the Basket.
Getting Started: Art Assets
As a prototype, this game doesn't need fantastic art; it needs to work. The kind of art
that you'll create throughout much of this book is known as programmer art, which is
the placeholder art made by programmers that will eventually be replaced by the actual
game art created by artists. As with nearly everything in a prototype, the purpose of this
art is to get you from a concept to a working prototype as quickly as possible. If your
programmer art doesn't look terrible, that's nice, but it's certainly not necessary.
AppleTree
Let's start with the tree.
1. From the Unity menu bar, choose GameObject > 3D Object > Cylinder. This will be the
trunk of the tree.

Camera Setup
One of the most important things to get right in your games is the position of the cam-
era. For Apple Picker, you want a camera that shows a decent-sized play area. Because
the gameplay in this game is entirely two dimensional, you also want an orthographic
camera instead of a perspective one. For more information on perspective and ortho-
graphic cameras, see the "Orthographic Versus Perspective Cameras" sidebar after
you've completed the following instructions. When finished, the settings for your Main
Camera Inspector should be the same as those shown in Figure 29.7a. In the figure, the
only settings you should need to change are highlighted.
1. Select Main Camera in the Hierarchy pane and ensure that its transform is set as
follows (you will probably only need to change the bolded Y position):
Main Camera (Camera) P:[ 0, 0, -10 ] R:[ 0, 0, 0 ] S:[ 1, 1, 1 ]
2. In the Camera component of the Inspector, set the following (as shown in
Figure 29.7a):
a. Set the Projection from Perspective to Orthographic.
b. Set the Size to 16 (Size only appears for orthographic cameras).
This makes the AppleTree a good size in the Game pane and leaves room for the apples
to fall and be caught by the player. Often, you can make a good first guess at things like
camera settings and then refine them after you've had a chance to play the game. Just
like everything else in game development, finding the right settings for the camera is

58172.heading: ORTHOGRAPHIC VERSUS PERSPECTIVE CAMERAS
58172.content:
ORTHOGRAPHIC VERSUS PERSPECTIVE CAMERAS
Orthographic and perspective are two types of virtual 3D cameras, as shown in
Figure 29.8.
A perspective camera works like the human eye; because light comes in through
a lens, objects that are close to the camera appear large, and objects that are far
away appear smaller. This gives a perspective camera a field of view (a.k.a. projec-
tion) shaped like a square frustum (or more simply, a square pyramid with the top
cut off). You can see this in the top half of Figure 29.8. The pyramidal wireframe
shape extending out from the camera is the view frustum and shows everything
that the camera will see.
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
PreParInG 635
Figure 29.8 Comparison of perspective and orthographic camera projections
Through an orthogonal camera, an object will appear to be the same size regard-
less of how far it is from the camera. The projection for an orthogonal camera is
rectangular rather than frustum shaped. This is shown in the bottom half of
Figure 29.8. The gray view frustum of an orthographic camera is a 3D rectangle
rather than a pyramid.
Earlier in the chapter, we set the Scene pane to 2D mode, which made the Scene
pane an orthographic camera looking straight down the Z axis. However, when

Game Panel Settings
Another contributing factor to your game view is the aspect ratio of the Game pane. The
aspect ratio is the relationship between the height and the width of the game view. The
orthographic Size that you just set in the Camera settings told Unity that there should
be 16m (i.e., 16 Unity units, which I sometimes abbreviate as meters) between the
center of the game view and the top and bottom edge of the view (for a total height of
32m). However, because of this, it's very important to be specific about the aspect ratio
of the Game pane as shown in Figure 29.9.
7
At the top of the Game pane is an aspect ratio pop-up menu that may currently display
Free Aspect. If so, this is something we need to fix:
1. Click the aspect ratio pop-up menu as shown in Figure 29.9.
2. Choose Full HD (1920x1080) from the menu.
1920x1080, or 1080p, is the standard "Full HD" resolution for high-definition television
and is the aspect ratio for many televisions and computer monitors. Unity's aspect ratio
menu also includes an option for 4K UHD (3840x2160) (or Ultra High Definition), which
is used by high-end modern console games, but for what we're doing—especially if you
the Scene pane is not locked in 2D mode, setting the Scene pane to be orthogonal
rather than perspective is also sometimes useful. To experiment with this:
■ Click the 2D button at the top of the Scene pane to exit 2D mode. This
will rotate into a 3D view of the scene.
■ Select the Main Camera so that you can see its rectangular frustum. This
will make the difference between the perspective and isometric scene
views clearer.
■ Click the word <Persp under the axes gizmo in the upper-right corner of
the Scene pane (shown in Figure 29.8). This will toggle the Scene pane
between perspective (abbreviated <Persp) and isometric (abbreviated =Iso)
scene views (isometric being another word for orthographic). Toggle
between the two a few times to see the difference.
■ Click the 2D button at the top of the Scene pane to return to 2D mode.
7. I have seen far too many projects look great inside the Unity editor on one computer and
absolutely awful on every other machine because the Game pane on the original computer
was set to Free Aspect. Don't do it!

■ Drop an apple every second.

The code that you'll enter into the AppleTree C# file is shown in Code Listing 29.1. The
first part of the script consists mostly of configuration variables, and you'll add more to

The code listings of other chapters often had line numbers preceding each line. The
scripts in this part of the book do not have line numbers because the scripts are long
enough that there would likely be variance between your line numbers and mine due to
differences in carriage returns over the course of many lines of code. However, the line
numbers also served a second purpose of helping you see the level of indent that the
line of code should be at (especially across page breaks). So, in place of the line num-
bers, I've added a pipe "|" to the beginning of each line. Please do not type the pipe.
It's just there to make the code more readable.
In all code listings, you'll also see bold right angle brackets " > " at the beginning of lines
that you need to type or modify. Again, please don't type the >; it's just there to help
you see what lines need your attention.

58184.heading: MAKING YOUR GAMES TIME BASED
58184.content:
MAKING YOUR GAMES TIME BASED
In nearly all game engines, the frame rate varies quite a bit throughout gameplay
as the engine endeavors to display new frames as quickly as possible while your
computer is also doing dozens of other tasks. If the movement in a game is frame-
based, these variances in the frame rate will affect your game, with the motion
speeding up when the frame rate is higher and slowing down when it's lower. On
the other hand, when the movement in a game is time-based, objects will move at
a consistent speed regardless of the frame rate at which the game is running. To
achieve this, we can use TiPe.deltaTiPe, a built-in Unity field that updates each
frame and tells us the number of seconds that have passed since the last frame.
TiPe.deltaTiPe is usually very small. For a game running at 25 fps (frames per
second), TiPe.deltaTiPe is 0.04f, meaning that each frame takes 4/100 of a sec-
ond to display. If the // c line of code were run when the frame rate was 25 fps,
the code would resolve like this:
pos.x += speed * Time.deltaTime;
pos.x += 1.0f * .f;
pos.x += 0.04f;
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
You might be wondering why lines // b through // d that you added to the
$ppleTree.8pdate() method were three lines instead of just one. Why couldn't
the code just be this?
transform.position.x += speed * Time.deltaTime;
The answer is that transforP.position is a property, a method that is masquerad-
ing as a field (i.e., a function masquerading as a variable) through the use of get^}
and set^} accessors (see Chapter 26, "Classes"). Although getting (i.e., reading) the
value of a property's subcomponent is possible, setting a subcomponent of a property
is not possible. In other words, transforP.position.[ can be read, but it cannot be
set directly. This necessitates the creation of the temporary 9ector pos that can be
modified and then assigned back to transforP.position.
2. Save the script, return to Unity, and press Play.
When you click the Play button, you'll notice that the AppleTree moves very slowly. Try
some different values for speed in the AppleTree Inspector and see what feels good to
you. I set speed to 10, which makes it move at 10m/s (10 meters per second or 10 Unity
units per second).
So, in 1/25 of a second, pos.[ would increase by 0.04m per frame. Over the
course of a full second, pos.[ would increase by 0.04m per frame * 25 frames, for
a total of 1 meter in 1 second.
If instead the game were running at 100 fps, it would resolve as follows:
pos.x += speed * Time.deltaTime;
pos.x += 1.0f * .1f;
pos.x += 0.01f;
So, in 1/100 of a second, pos.[ would increase by 0.01m per frame. Over the
course of a full second, pos.[ would increase by 0.01m per frame * 100 frames,
for a total of 1 meter in 1 second.

programming for mobile devices because the speed and power of mobile devices

change during playback without affecting the saved scene; but in this case,
you must make sure that the speed of AppleTree is set to what you want it to
be (e.g., 10) when Unity is not in play mode.
Changing Direction
Now that the AppleTree is moving at a decent rate, it will run off of the screen pretty
quickly. Let's make it change directions when it hits the left$ndRightEdge value.
1. Modify the AppleTree script in Code Listing 29.3 by adding the bold lines following

positive speed value translates into movement to the right.

Mathf.$bs(speed), ensuring that the AppleTree will move to the left.

an opening and closing screen, you can add these things yourself after you gain more
experience.

future. One of the best ways to learn coding is to follow a tutorial like this chapter and
then try to add your own modifications to it.

image and a Start button. The Start button could then call SceneManager./oad

top of your script. You will also need to open the File > Build Settings… window in
Unity and add the Start Screen scene to the build (and also _Scene_0, if you didn't
do it as part of the Standard Project Setup Procedure from Appendix A).

58225.content:
MISSION DEMOLITION
Physics games are some of the most popular
around, making games like Angry Birds
household names. In this chapter, you make
your own physics game that is inspired by
Angry Birds and all the other physics games that
came before it, such as Crossbows and Catapults,
Worms, Scorched Earth, and so on.
This chapter covers the following: physics,
collisions, mouse interaction, levels, and game

682 CHAPTER 30 MISSION DEMOLITION
What You Will Learn
As the first in our series of tutorials, you'll learn several new concepts and review some
from Part II of the book, including:
■ Using vector math to fire a projectile
■ Importing pixel art assets from a UnityPackage (the clouds)
■ Working with prefabs and nested prefabs to make complex but changeable
GameObjects
■ Using the LineRenderer component to draw configurable trails for objects
■ Tracking and loading multiple levels
■ Using buttons in the uGUI user interface system
■ Converting a Collider to a trigger for sensing the end of a level
Figure 30.1 Mission Demolition as it will be at the end of this chapter
The Mission Demolition Prototype
This game is a simple version of a style of physics-based game that has been very
popular for decades. In our version, the player can launch a projectile from the slingshot
on the left at the castle on the right, with the goal of the projectile touching the green
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
Game PrototyPe ConCePt 683
goal box. We'll make a few different models of castle and will write code for managing
the camera view, keeping track of levels and the number of shots taken, randomizing
cloud positions, and implementing a line that tracks the projectile and shows where the
player's previous shots have gone.
Getting Started: Mission Demolition
Because this is the second prototype and you now have some experience under your
belt, this chapter is going to move a bit faster than the previous one when covering
things that you have already experienced. Of course, I still cover new topics in detail.

58227.content:
SET UP THE PROJECT FOR THIS CHAPTER
Following the standard project setup procedure, create a new project in Unity. If
you need a refresher on the standard project setup procedure, see Appendix A,
"Standard Project Setup Procedure."
■ Project Template: 3D Core
■ Project Name: Mission Demolition
■ Scene Name: _Scene_0
■ Game Pane Dimensions: Full HD (1920x1080)
Game Prototype Concept
In this game, the player uses a slingshot to fire projectiles at a castle, hoping to demolish
it. Each castle has a goal area that the projectile must touch for the player to continue to
the next level.
This is the desired sequence of events:
1. When the player's mouse pointer is in range of the slingshot, the slingshot should
glow.
2. If the player presses the left mouse button (mouse button 0 in Unity) down while the
slingshot is glowing, a projectile will instantiate at the location of the mouse pointer.
3. As the player moves and drags the mouse around with the button held down, the
projectile follows it, yet remains within a specific distance of the slingshot.

5. When the player releases mouse button 0, the projectile fires from the slingshot.
6. The player's goal is to knock down a castle that is several meters away and hit a
target area inside.
7. The player has a total of three shots to hit the goal. The most recent shot will leave a
trail so that the player can better judge their next shot.
Many of the preceding events relate to mechanics, but one is exclusively aesthetics:
step 4. All the other elements that mention art use that art for the purpose of game
mechanics, but step 4 is just to make the game look nicer, so it's less critical to the pro-
totype. When you're writing down your concepts for games, this is an important thing
to keep in mind. That isn't to say that you shouldn't implement things that are entirely
aesthetics in a prototype; you just need to be aware of and prioritize the elements that
will have the most direct impact on the game mechanics. For the sake of time and space,
this prototype focuses on the other elements, and I leave the implementation of step 4
for you to tackle later.

Coding the Prototype
With the art assets in place, it's time to start adding code to this project. The first script to
add is one for Slingshot that will cause it to react to mouse input, instantiate a Projectile,
and fire that Projectile instance. You will write this script in an iterative manner by add-
ing only small sections of code at a time, testing the code, and then adding a little more.
When you start creating your own scripts, this is a fantastic way to approach them: Imple-
ment something small and easy to code, test it, implement another small thing, repeat.

58243.heading: COLLISION DETECTION: DISCRETE VS. CONTINUOUS
58243.content:
COLLISION DETECTION: DISCRETE VS. CONTINUOUS
If you look at the Rigidbody component, you'll see that there is a pop-up menu for
selecting Collision Detection. By setting the collisionDetectionMode of a Rigid-
body, we're setting the same thing. Here's an explanation for the different values:
■ Discrete: The Rigidbody only checks collisions in each FixedUpdate. This
is the most efficient, but it also can mean that if a fast-moving projectile is
on one side of a thin wall in one FixedUpdate and on the other side in the
next FixedUpdate (but doesn't touch the wall in either frame), discrete
mode will not see the collision at all.
■ Continuous: This is more accurate for fast-moving objects like the pro-
jectile because it checks for collisions in between FixedUpdates. However,
it takes more processor power to do this.
■ Continuous Dynamic: If you were making a billiards game with several
fast-moving balls, each ball would need to be set to Continuous Dynamic
in order to collide accurately with the others. This is because the preced-
ing Continuous mode only checks the moving object against the static
(unmoving) positions of other objects in the frame. Continuous Dynamic
is needed when you want to see if two fast-moving objects collide with
each other. This, of course, takes significantly more processing power
than any other mode.
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
CodInG the PrototyPe 699
■ Continuous Speculative: This mode is needed if you want to treat
a kinematic Rigidbody as if it has Continuous collision detection. The
other forms of Continuous collision detection rely on the velocity of the
Rigidbody to check for collisions between frames, but a kinematic Rigid-
body doesn't use its velocity, so Continuous Speculative uses different
calculations to speculate (i.e., guess) at what the kinematic Rigidbody hit
between frames. This is actually less processor-intensive than the other
forms of Continuous detection, but it is also less accurate.
In prior editions of the book, we just set the Collision Detection for the Projectile
to Continuous and left it at that, but in more recent versions of Unity, if you set a
Rigidbody with Continuous collision detection to is.inePatic, Unity will throw a
warning into the Console, so I wanted to show you how to set collisionDetection-
Mode in code and avoid this warning.
For more information about the types of collision detection, click the help icon in
the top-right corner of the Rigidbody component.

Figure 30.8 Two-dimensional vector subtraction: A minus B looks at A
As you can see in Figure 30.8, vectors are added and subtracted one component at a
time (meaning that the x and y dimensions are handled separately). The figure is two
dimensional, but the same methods work for 3D. The x components of the vectors A
and B are subtracted independently from the y components, making a new Vector2
that is Vector2( 2-5, 8-3 ), which becomes Vector2( -3, 5 ). The figure illustrates that A-B
gives us the vector distance between A and B (with the vector's root at [0,0], also known
as the origin). This same vector result is also the distance and direction that one must
move to get from point B to point A. A mnemonic to remember which one the vector
will point at is "A minus B looks at A."

Making a Follow Camera
You need _MainCamera to follow the projectile when it is launched, but the behavior is
a little more complicated than that. The eventual full behavior should be as follows:
A. The camera sits at an initial position and doesn't move during Slingshot's
aimingMode.
B. After the projectile is launched, the camera follows it (with a little easing to make it
follow the projectile with a bit of a smooth lag; we'll cover this soon).
C. As the camera moves up into the air, increase the Camera.orthographicSize to keep
the ground in view.
D. When the projectile comes to rest, the camera stops following it and returns to the
initial position.
To begin with, let's just get the camera moving at all, and we'll iteratively add more
functionality as we go. The following code will enable the camera to follow a POI (Point
of Interest) GameObject. We will later set that POI in the Slingshot code.
1. Select _MainCamera in the Hierarchy.
2. To create a new FollowCam script and add it to _MainCamera at the same time:
a. Click the Add Component button at the bottom of the _MainCamera Inspector.
b. Type FollowCam into the search bar that appears. This will not find a pre-
existing FollowCam script, so it will give you the option to create a new script.
c. Click New script.
d. Double-check the FollowCam name and then click Create and Add.
The process in step 2 will create a new FollowCam script in the Assets folder of the Proj-
ect pane and also add that FollowCam script to _MainCamera as a Component. This is a
newer workflow in Unity that I've personally been using a lot. The only negative is that
it places the new script in the top-level of the Assets folder in the Project pane, so you
will need to manually move the script into a __Scripts folder, if you have one.

Issue B: The Projectile Doesn't Bounce Realistically
To fix issue B, you must add both Rigidbody constraints and a Physic Material to the
Projectile prefab:
1. Select the Projectile prefab in the Project pane.
2. In the Projectile Rigidbody component:
a. Open the disclosure triangle next to Constraints.
b. Set the check box next to Freeze Position Z to true.
c. Set the check boxes next to Freeze Rotation X, Y, and Z to true.
Freeze Position Z keeps the projectile from moving toward or away from the camera
(basically keeping it in the same Z depth as both the ground and the castle that will be
added later). Freeze Rotation X, Y, and Z keeps it from rolling around.
3. Save the scene, click Play, and try launching the projectile again.
These Rigidbody settings keep the projectile from rolling endlessly, but it still doesn't
feel right. You've spent your whole life experiencing physics, and that gives you an intui-
tive feel for the kinds of behaviors that feel like natural, real-world physics. This is true
for your players as well, which means that even though physics is a complex system that
requires a lot of math to model, if you make your game physics feel like the physics that
players are used to, you won't have to explain that math to them. Adding a Physic Mate-
rial can make your physically simulated objects feel a lot more realistic.
4. From the Unity menu bar, choose Assets > Create > Physic Material.
5. Name this Physic material PhysMat_Projectile.

2. Adjust the Sleep Threshold of the Unity Physics settings:
a. Choose Edit > Project Settings from the main Unity menu, and select the Physics
tab (not Physics 2D).
b. Change Sleep Threshold from 0.005 to 0.01, and close the Project Settings
window.
The Sleep Threshold is the amount of movement in a single physics engine frame that
will cause a Rigidbody to continue to be simulated in the following frame. If an object
moves less than this amount (which we've now set to 1cm) in a single frame, PhysX will
sleep that Rigidbody object and cease simulating it (i.e., stop moving the GameObject).
The Rigidbody will only come out of sleep if something happens to make it move again
(e.g., it's hit by another object or the floor it is resting on is removed).

Providing Vection and a Sense of Speed
The FollowCam moves pretty well now, but it's still difficult to tell how fast the projec-
tile is moving, especially when it's high in the air. To fix this issue, let's take advantage of
the concept of vection. Vection is the sensation of movement that you get from seeing
other things passing by quickly, and it is the concept that led to parallax scrolling in
2D video games. Parallax scrolling causes foreground objects to pass by quickly while
background objects move more slowly relative to the movement of the main camera in
a 2D game. Although a full parallax system is beyond the scope of this tutorial, you can

I use RandoP.Range() for many things in Code Listing 30.12, so I wanted to make

The int version of RandoP.Range is inclusive of the min value but exclusive of
the max value. This means that RandoP.Range(   ) will return one of the
numbers [ 0, 1, 2, 3 ], but it will never return 4.
int RandoP.Range(int Pin int Pa[) —The int version of RandoP.Range()
includes the min number but excludes the max number. So, for example, RandoP.
Range(   ) will randomly choose between the numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4, but
will never choose 5. This is very useful for arrays like the cloudSprites array in Code
Listing 30.12. When choosing a cloud sprite on line // e of the code listing,
RandoP.Range(  cloudSprites./ength ) is called, which will return one of
the numbers 0–4, which are all of the valid indices for the cloudSprites array.
Arrays are one of the main reasons that the max value in the int version of
RandoP.Range() is excluded.
float RandoP.Range(float Pin float Pa[) —The float version of RandoP.
Range() includes the min number and includes the max number. So, for example,
RandoP.Range( f 1f ) will randomly choose any floating point number
between 0 and 1, including 0 and 1. (Note that in this example call, either  or
1 needed the f after it, or this would have been seen as an int call to RandoP.
Range(  1 ), which always returns .)
RandoP.Range() with two Vector 3s —The RandoPPos() method in Code
Listing 30.12 returns any point that is within the volume (i.e., box) with PinPos at
the bottom-left near corner of the volume and Pa[Pos at the top-right far corner.
In Mission Demolition, this gives us a volume in which the clouds will spawn. The
variance in Z position means that some clouds will be closer to the camera and
others further away. Choosing min and max Z values on either side of the Projec-

Organizing the Project Pane
Now that you've created many different assets and scripts, it's time to talk about orga-

Project pane. I usually do this at the very beginning of a project but have waited until
now on this project so that you can experience how much better the project feels
when it's organized. You can create folders as needed for each project, though I always
include a __Scripts folder to keep all my scripts organized.

Making a Goal Using Nested Prefabs
The final GameObject to add to Castle is a goal for the player to hit with the projectile.
We're also going to use this section to teach you more about nested prefabs, which are
the reason that the Prefab Mode of the Scene pane arrived in Unity 2018.3.
In previous versions of Unity, whenever you made a prefab, every child of that prefab
became exclusively a part of that prefab, including any GameObjects that were formerly

we made the Castle into a prefab—as we did in step 10—the Walls and Slabs that were
its children would lose any connection to the Wall and Slab prefabs from which they'd
been built. So changing the scale of Slab (in step 11) would not change the Slabs that
were part of Castle, because they were no longer Slab instances.
After many years of requests from game developers and lots of work by the Unity team,
nested prefabs launched in 2018.3 and are now an important part of a good Unity
workflow.
The following steps will not be the most efficient way to add a Goal to the Castle, but
they will show you a bit about how to use nested prefabs.
1. Add a Goal cube to the Castle instance in the Hierarchy by right-clicking on the word
Castle in the Hierarchy and choosing 3D Object > Cube from the pop-up menu. This
creates a new Cube as a child of Castle.
2. Rename the Cube to Goal.
If you deselect Goal, you can see that Goal has a black cube outline icon because it is not
a prefab instance. It also has a plus superimposed over its icon, showing that it is some-
thing that you have added to this instance that is not part of the Castle prefab. Unity
now allows these kinds of modifications to a prefab instance and calls them overrides.
3. Click Castle in the Hierarchy and then click the Overrides button near the top of the
Castle Inspector pane. There, you'll see Goal listed as an instance override of the
Castle prefab.
4. In this same Overrides pop-up, click the Apply All button. This applies all overrides on
this instance back to the prefab itself. Now, the name of Goal is blue in the Hierarchy
and the plus has disappeared because Goal is now part of the Castle prefab.
5. Try dragging Goal into the _Prefabs folder of the Project pane to make it its own
prefab, and you'll get an error: "Cannot restructure Prefab instance." To make struc-
tural changes to a prefab (like changing a child of it from a regular GameObject to a
prefab instance), you need to use the Prefab Mode of the Scene pane.

Testing the Castle
To test the castle, do the following:
1. Select the Castle instance in the Hierarchy and set its position to P:[ 50, -9.5, 0 ].
2. Click Play and try to knock the Castle down with a Projectile.
You might have to fire a few times to get it, but you can see how the game will work. If
you're unlucky, the Projectile might get in a position where it doesn't ever sleep. Even
if the Projectile is moving less than 0.01m, this can happen when multiple objects are
touching and any of them are not sleeping. We'll deal with this next.
Fixing Rigidbody's Insomnia
As just mentioned, when the Projectile gets jumbled in with the Walls and Slabs, it
sometimes never goes to sleep, which means that we could wait a very long time
before we can take another shot. We need to have more control over when the Pro-
jectile sleeps, so we'll write our own method to track the distance that the Projectile
has moved each FixedUpdate, and if the Projectile has moved less than 0.01m for ten
consecutive frames, we'll decide to treat it as if it's asleep.
1. Add a new Projectile script to the Projectile prefab:
a. Select the Projectile prefab in the Project pane.
b. Click the Add Component button at the bottom of the Projectile Inspector.
c. Type Projectile into the Add Component search box and click New script.
d. Click Create and Add.

PUBLIC GET, PRIVATE SET PROPERTIES
In Code Listing 30.14, we set up an aZaNe property that has a public get clause
but a priYate set clause (preventing other scripts from setting it). This is a very
common pattern to allow any class to see the value of a property like aZaNe with-
out giving them the ability to edit it.
One Unity-specific issue with this is that properties can't be seen or modified in
the Inspector. If we want to also interact with the aZaNe value in the Unity Inspec-
tor, we need to create a private backing field for the property (BaZaNe in this
example) and give it the >Seriali]e)ield@ Compiler Attribute, which tells Unity
to show this value in the Inspector (and to let you alter it there) even though
BaZaNe is private.
For more information on Compiler Attributes, see the "C# and Unity Coding
Concepts: Attributes" section of Appendix B.
Adding a ProjectileLine Trail
Although Unity does have a built-in TrailRenderer effect, it won't really serve our pur-
pose for Mission Demolition because we need more control over the trail than it allows.
Instead, we'll make use of the LineRenderer upon which the Trail Renderer is built.
First, we'll create a separate ProjectileLine GameObject that will contain a LineRenderer
component, and then we'll use Slingshot to create an instance of the ProjectileLine
prefab as a child of each Projectile that is fired.

ProjectileLine.

Now that you have a goal and can hit it with the Projectile, this is what I would call a

58294.heading: ENUM
58294.content:
ENUM
An enum (or enumeration) is a way of defining specific, named numbers in C#.
The enum definition at the top of the MissionDemolition C# script declares an
enum type GaPeMode with three potential values: idle, playing, and leYelEnd.
After you define an enum, you can then declare a variable that uses the defined
enum as its type.
public GameMode mode = GameMode.idle;
The preceding line creates a new variable named Pode that is of the type
GaPeMode and has the value GaPeMode.idle.
You often use enums in code when only a few specific options exist for a variable
and you want those options to be easily readable by humans. Alternatively, passing
the type of game mode as a string (e.g., "idle", "playing", or "levelEnd") would be
possible, but the enum is a much cleaner way of doing this that isn't as susceptible
to misspelling and that allows for autocomplete while typing.
For more information about enums, see Appendix B, "Useful Concepts."

Summary
That's it for the Mission Demolition prototype. In just one chapter, you've made a
physics-based game like Angry Birds that you can continue to improve and expand on
your own. This and all the following tutorials are really meant to be frameworks on top
of which you can build whatever game you want.

58303.content:
752 CHAPTER 30 MISSION DEMOLITION
Next Steps
You could add a ton of additional features, some of which include the following:
■ Use PlayerPrefs to store the best score, as you did in Apple Picker. In this game, it
would probably be scored like Golf where the player is trying to complete all levels
in as few shots as possible.
■ Make the castle parts out of various materials, some of which would have more or
less mass. Some materials could even break if struck hard enough (by break, I mean
disappear; actual destructible meshes are very complex to implement). When work-
ing with materials like this, don't forget that you can use a Physic Material to choose
how bouncy a Collider is.
■ Use a Line Renderer to draw the rubber band of the slingshot.
■ Add more background elements like mountains or buildings, and implement
movement or even actual parallax scrolling on the background clouds. You could
also tie that parallax scrolling to the scale and z position of the clouds, with larger
clouds closer and faster moving while smaller clouds would be further away and
move more slowly. We will implement simple parallax scrolling Chapter 32, "Space
SHMUP – Part 2."
■ Anything else you want!
After you've worked your way through the other prototypes in this book, come back
to this one and think about what you could add to it. Create your own designs, show
them to people, and iterate to make the game better. Remember that design is always
an iterative process. If you make a change you don't like, don't let it discourage you; just
chalk it up to experience and try something else.
It's also worth repeating here that it's okay if you don't completely understand every-
thing that we did in the code in this chapter. I often liken learning C# to learning any
normal human language, while also solving a bunch of logic puzzles. When learning
Spanish, Mandarin, or French, there is a lot of repetition, some of which you're not
going to understand at the time, but immersion within that language and seeing it used
will help you to eventually learn it much better (and faster!). These tutorials are that kind
of repetition for Unity and C#. It's okay if you don't understand exactly what's going on
with each step as long as you get the general idea. Later, when you want to do some-
thing like add a trail behind a moving GameObject that is more configurable than a
standard Trail Renderer would allow, you'll remember this project and can return to it to
copy and modify how we did it here.

58305.content:
SPACE SHMUP – PART 1
The SHMUP (or shoot 'em up) game genre
includes such classic games as Galaga and
Galaxian from the 1980s and the more modern
masterpiece Ikaruga.
In this chapter, you create a SHMUP using
several programming techniques that will
serve you well throughout your programming
and prototyping careers. These include class
inheritance, static fields and methods, the
singleton pattern, and delegates. Though
you've seen many of these techniques before,
you will use them more extensively in this
prototype.
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
754 CHAPTER 31 SPACE SHMUP – Part 1
What You Will Learn
This chapter covers several new concepts and reviews many others. These include:
■ Importing and using a UnityPackage full of art assets for this game
■ Working with art assets that were not made in Unity
■ Creating custom resolutions for the Game pane
■ Using Input Axes to smooth player character motion
■ Setting texture coordinates to show only part of an image
■ Using /ate8pdate() to react to limit player movement
■ Spawning enemies at random positions
■ And much more!
Figure 31.1 Two views of the Space SHMUP game prototype showing the results of the Part 1
and Part 2 chapters. The player is using the blaster weapon in the left image and the spread weapon
in the right.

Getting Started: Space SHMUP
In this project, you make a prototype for a classic space-based SHMUP. To give you a head
start in this chapter, you will start with many of the models and assets partially pre-made,
though I have included places where you will need to compose or modify those assets to
help teach you a bit about importing assets in Unity. Figure 31.1 shows an image of what
the finished prototype will look like at the end of this chapter and the next. The images
show the player ship at the bottom of the screen (surrounded by a green shield) as well
as several enemy types and an upgrade (the power-up cube marked S).

SET UP THE PROJECT FOR THIS CHAPTER
Following the standard project setup procedure, create a new project in Unity. If
you need a refresher on this procedure, see Appendix A, "Standard Project Setup
Procedure."
■ Project Template: 3D Core
■ Project Name: Space SHMUP Part 1
■ Starter UnityPackage: Find Chapter 31 at http://book.prototools.net

_Prefabs

Importing a Unity Asset Package
One new thing in the setup for this prototype is that you must download and import
a custom Unity asset package. The creation of complex art and imagery for games is
beyond the scope of this book, but I've created a package of some fantastic starships by
Peter Burroughs
1
as well as other assets that will allow you to create all the visual effects
required for this game. Of course, as mentioned several times throughout this book, when
you're making a prototype, how it plays and feels are much more important than how it
looks, but having an understanding of how to work with art assets is still important.
The instructions for downloading and installing a Starter UnityPackage as required for
this chapter are in Appendix A, "Standard Project Setup Procedure." Follow those to
import the IGDPD3e.C31_Space_SHMUP_Starter.unitypackage for this chapter. The
Import Unity Package window for this chapter is shown in Figure 31.2a.
1. To learn more about Peter's work, check out his website at https://kairosmith.com/.

Select all the files as shown in Figure 31.2a (by clicking the All button), and click Import.
This imports a __Scene_0, places four new textures and one new shader into the
_Materials folder, and includes many models, textures, and other assets in the Assets by
Peter Burroughs folder.
Textures are usually just image files. The creation of textures is beyond the scope of this
book, but many books and online tutorials cover texture creation. Adobe Photoshop is
probably the most commonly used image editing tool, but it is very expensive. A com-
mon open source alternative is Gimp (http://www.gimp.org), and a good new com-
mercial competitor is Affinity Photo (https://affinity.serif.com/photo). By far, the easiest
image editor to access is Photopea (pronounced Photo-pee), which is an entirely free
online tool that reproduces most of the capabilities of Photoshop in a web browser. You
can find it at https://www.photopea.com/.

The creation of shaders is also far beyond the scope of this book. Shaders are programs
that tell your computer how to render a texture on a GameObject. They can make a
scene look realistic, cartoony, or however else you like, and they are an important part
of the graphics of any modern game. Traditionally, Unity used its own unique shader
language called ShaderLab,
2
though most recent shader development is done in
ShaderGraph,
3
a visual scripting engine for shaders that can produce fantastic results.
The included UnlitAlpha.shader shader is a simple one that bypasses most of the
things a shader can do to simply render a colored, non-lit shape on the screen with
alpha blending and transparency, and I wrote it in ShaderLab years ago. For on-screen
elements that you want to be a specific bright color, this custom UnlitAlpha shader is
perfect. We'll use UnlitAlpha for the power-up cubes in this game (and differentiate it
from the Unlit shaders that are included with Unity).

58313.heading: INPUT AXES AND THE INPUT MANAGER
58313.content:
INPUT AXES AND THE INPUT MANAGER
Much of the code in the Hero.8pdate() code listing should look familiar to you,
though this is the first time in the book that you've seen the Input.Get$[is()
method. Unity's Input Manager allows you to configure various input axes, and
those axes can be read through Input.Get$[is(). To view the default Input axes,
choose Edit > Project Settings… from the menu bar and then choose Input Manager
from the left sidebar. You will probably need to click the disclosure triangle next to
Axes to show all of them, as shown in Figure 31.4.
Figure 31.4 Unity's Input Manager showing the default Horizontal axis settings (split in two
halves; the first for keyboard, and the second for joystick)
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
makInG the hero shIP 763
One thing to note about the settings in Figure 31.4 is that several axis names are
listed twice (e.g., Horizontal, Vertical, and Jump). As you can see in the expanded
view of the two Horizontal axes in the figure, this allows the Horizontal axis to be
controlled by either presses on the keyboard (accepting left and right arrow as
well as A and D, as shown in the left image of Figure 31.4) or a joystick axis (shown
in the right image). This is one of the great strengths of the input axes; several
different types of input can control a single axis. As a result, your games only need
one line to read the value of an axis rather than a line to handle joystick input, a
line for each arrow key, and a line each for the A and D keys.
Every call to Input.Get$[is() returns a float between − 1 and 1 in value (with
a default of 0). Each axis in the Input Manager also includes values for Sensitivity
and Gravity, though these are only used for Key or Mouse Button input (see the left
image of Figure 31.4). Sensitivity and Gravity cause the axis value to interpolate
smoothly when a key is pressed or released. (That is, instead of immediately jump-
ing to the final value, the axis value will blend from the original value to the final
value over time.) In the Horizontal axis shown, a sensitivity of 3 means that when
the right-arrow key is pressed, it takes 1/3 of a second for the value to interpolate
from 0 to 1. A gravity of 3 means that when the right-arrow key is released, it takes
1/3 of a second for the axis value to interpolate back to 0. The higher the sensitiv-
ity or gravity, the faster the interpolation takes place.
The effect of the Snap setting is subtle but important. When Snap is false (unchecked),
if the Horizontal axis is currently − 1 (i.e., fully left), and you press and hold the right
arrow key, the value will smoothly interpolate back to 0 and then to 1. On the other
hand, when Snap is true (the default), if the Horizontal axis is currently − 1, and you

and more reactive, but it may not be what you want for all games.
As with many things in Unity, you can find out a lot more about the Input Man-
ager by clicking the Help button (that looks like a gray circle with a question mark
and is to the right of the name Input Manager at the top of the Project Settings
window).
Starting in 2020, Unity released a new Input System as a package in the Package
Manager, but I have chosen to not use it in this book. While the new Input System
is excellent at handling input from multiple game pads on the same machine and
at making input consistent across several brands of game pads (e.g., Microsoft,
Sony, Nintendo), it takes much more effort to configure and is not needed for the
keyboard and mouse input used throughout this book.

your game, and you should have settings that feel right to you. Make changes as

Part of what makes this feel nice is the apparent inertia that the ship carries. When you
release the movement key, the ship takes a little while to slow down. Similarly, upon
pressing a movement key, the ship takes a little while to get up to speed. This apparent
movement inertia is caused by the Sensitivity, Gravity, and Snap axis settings that are
described in the sidebar. Changing these settings in the Input Manager affect the
movement and maneuverability of _Hero.

Keeping _Hero on Screen
The motion of your _Hero ship should feel pretty good now, and the rotating shield
looks nice, but at this point, you can easily fly the ship off the screen. To resolve this,
you're going to make a reusable component script.
6
You can read more about the
Component Pattern of software design in Chapter 27, "Object-Oriented Thinking," and
under "Object-Oriented Software Design Patterns" in Appendix B, "Useful Concepts."
In brief, a component is a small piece of code that is meant to work alongside oth-
ers to add functionality to a GameObject without conflicting with other code on the
object. All of Unity's built-in components that you've worked with in the Inspector (e.g.,
Renderer, Transform, and so on) all follow this pattern.

58320.heading: Chapter 26, "Classes," covered a bit about the Enemy class and subclasses for a game
58320.content:
Chapter 26, "Classes," covered a bit about the Enemy class and subclasses for a game
like this. There you learned about setting up a superclass for all enemies that can be
extended by its subclasses. For this game, you will extend that further in the next
chapter, but first, let's create the artwork.
Enemy Artwork
The hero has a very warm gold tone, so to contrast this, the enemies were modeled
with cool blues and purples. Enemies are also round to contrast with the hero ship's
more angular aesthetic. You can see all five enemies in Figure 31.5, though we'll only
implement Enemy_0 in this chapter.
Figure 31.5 Each of the five enemy ship types
Preparing Enemy_0 for the game is very similar to the process you used to get _Hero
ready, though we'll do it in a slightly different order:
1. Create an empty GameObject named Enemy_0.
a. Choose GameObject > Create Empty from the Unity menu.
b. Rename the GameObject to Enemy_0.
c. Set the Enemy_0 transform to P:[ 0, 20, 0 ], R:[ 0, 0, 0 ], S:[ 1.5, 1.5, 1.5 ].
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
772 CHAPTER 31 SPACE SHMUP – Part 1
2. Drag the enemy0 model from the Assets by Peter Burroughs > Models folder onto
Enemy_0 in the Hierarchy, making it a child of Enemy_0.
a. Set the transform of the enemy0 child to P:[ 0, 0, 0 ], R:[ 90, 180, 0 ], S:[ 0.01,
0.01, 0.01 ].
Now, we need to add the components that will allow this enemy to work in the game.
All of these will be attached to the Enemy_0 root-level GameObject, not to its enemy0
child.
3. Select Enemy_0 at the root level of the Hierarchy and add a Capsule Collider.
a. Double-click Enemy_0 in the Hierarchy to focus on it in the Scene view. You may
want to click the 2D button at the top of the Scene view to view Enemy_0 from
the same orientation as the orthographic _MainCamera.
b. With Enemy_0 selected, click the Add Component button and add a Capsule Col-
lider (you can find it under Physics > or by typing "Capsule" into the search bar).
c. Set the Capsule Collider Radius to 1.2.
d. Set the Capsule Collider Height to 2.9.
You should see that the Capsule Collider now completely surrounds Enemy_0. There is
some empty space within the Capsule Collider, but a good thing to remember is that
players will be much more upset if they think they hit an enemy but the shot didn't
register than if they think they missed but the shot did register, so it's always better for
enemies to err on the side of making the colliders for enemies too large. On the other
hand, for the player themselves, they'll rarely complain if they think they were probably
supposed to get hit, but the game doesn't count it. So always make your colliders for
the player smaller or make it very clear where the boundary is (as we've done with the
circular shield).

a. Select Enemy_0 in the Hierarchy and choose Component > Physics > Rigidbody

GameObject and all of its children are updated every frame.

We'll do this by creating an enum with the >SysteP.)lags@ compiler attribute. With
the Flags attribute, if the value of each enum member is set to be a power of two (e.g.,
0, 1, 2, 4, 8), then that enum will be able to hold multiple values at the same time.

58327.content:
USING BITWISE OPERATORS WITH SYSTEM.FLAGS ENUMS
If an enum has the >SysteP.)lags@ compiler attribute, then it will be able to
hold multiple values at the same time. >SysteP.)lags@ enums are also some-
times called bitmasks because you can think of each binary bit (i.e., an individual 0
or 1 in a variable) in the enum as representing a single value being true or false.
For example, the /ayerMasN type in Unity is a >SysteP.)lags@ enum, with each
of the binary bits of the 32-bit enum representing one of the 32 possible Lay-
ers being enabled or disabled. You can see this by selecting _MainCamera in the
scene Hierarchy and looking in the Camera component of the Inspector at the Cull-
ing Mask pop-up menu. By default, Culling Mask is set to Everything and includes
all Layers (meaning that the Camera will render GameObjects on all Layers), but
you can also individually turn Layers on and off because the /ayerMasN culling
MasN is a Flags enum.
The >SysteP.)lags@ enuP eScreen/ocs will work in a similar way. The value
of each of the defined off screen positions is a different power of 2, as shown in
Figure 31.7b. Because these are powers of 2 (i.e., 0, 1, 2, 4, & 8), they each can be
represented by a single bit in the enum.
As Figure 31.7a shows, when a GameObject is off screen to the right, its eScreen
/ocs value is offRight, which is stored as the 1 bit (a decimal value of 1).
off8p is stored as the 1 bit (with a decimal value of 4). If a GameObject is both
offRight and off8p, then the eScreen/ocs value will be 11 (a decimal value
of 5), holding both offRight and off8p in a single enum value.

However, right now, when the _Hero collides with an enemy, nothing happens. This

Setting Tags, Layers, and Physics
As was presented in Chapter 29, " Apple Picker," one of the things that layers control in
Unity is which objects do or do not collide with each other. First, let's think about the
Space SHMUP prototype. In this game, several different types of GameObjects could be
placed on five distinct layers that will interact with each other in different ways:
■ Hero: The _Hero ship should collide with enemies, enemy projectiles, and power-
ups but should not collide with hero projectiles.
■ Enemy: Enemies should collide with _Hero and hero projectiles but not with
power-ups.
■ ProjectileHero: Projectiles fired by _Hero should only collide with enemies.

■ ProjectileEnemy: Projectiles fired by enemies should only collide with _Hero.

■ PowerUp: Power-ups should only collide with _Hero.
To create these layers, complete these steps:
1. Open the Tags & Layers manager in the Project Settings window by selecting Edit >
Project Settings… from the Unity menu and then clicking Tags and Layers on the left
side. Tags and physics layers are different from each other, but both are set in the
same window.
2. Open the disclosure triangle next to Layers. Builtin Layers 0–2, 4, and 5 are reserved
by Unity, but you can set the names of User Layers 3 and 6–31. Starting with User
Layer 8 (to give us some space from the Unity ones), enter the layer names shown in
Figure 31.8.
The Layer names are Hero, Enemy, ProjectileHero, ProjectileEnemy, and PowerUp.

58346.content:
SPACE SHMUP – PART 2
In this chapter, you add power-ups, multiple
enemies, and different weapon types to the
Space SHMUP game. In doing so, you learn
more about class inheritance, enums, function
delegates, and several other important topics.
As an added bonus, you also make the game a
lot more fun!

808 CHAPTER 32 SPACE SHMUP – Part 2
What You Will Learn
This chapter covers several new concepts and reviews many others. These include:
■ Implementing five different Enemy types using class inheritance
■ Setting the likelihood of various Enemies appearing and dropping various power-ups
■ Understanding more about private, protected, and public fields and methods
■ Using an AnimationCurve to rotate a GameObject with precision over time
■ Implementing two different weapon types and three power-up types
■ Allowing the player to have up to five weapons of each type
■ Using multicast C# delegate events to fire all weapons with a single call

SET UP THE PROJECT FOR THIS CHAPTER
Rather than following the standard project setup procedure, you will need to con-

■ You can continue working in the project folder from the previous chapter.
■ You can make a duplicate of your project folder from the previous chap-

a class and need to turn the two chapters in separately—it can be useful

background of the same File Explorer window and choose Paste.

Space SHMUP Part 2.

new project folder and open it.
