the Project Settings window (Edit > Project Settings…) and click the Player
tab on the left side of the window. Then, change the Product Name to Space

WHAT IF YOUR NEW ENEMY_0 DOESN'T ACT EXACTLY LIKE ENEMY?
Because EnePyB is a subclass of EnePy, it inherits all the non-private
methods, fields, properties, and other elements of EnePy, but Visual Studio
has an annoying habit of automatically making methods priYate. Open
the EnePy class and make sure that all built-in methods (e.g., $ZaNe(),
8pdate(), and 2n&ollisionEnter()) are just preceded by Yoid (not
priYate Yoid). Also, please double-check that the MoYe() method is
declared as public Yirtual Yoid MoYe().
The other very common mistake that I see in my students' work is that they
will neglect to delete the Start() and 8pdate() methods from EnePyB.
EnePyB —as well as all the other Enemy subclasses you'll write in this
chapter—relies on the 8pdate() method from EnePy to call MoYe(), and if
this doesn't happen, EnePyB will not move.

Preparing for the Other Enemies
The remaining enemies make use of linear interpolation, an important development
concept that is described in Appendix B. You saw a very simple interpolation for the
FollowCam.cs code that moved the Camera in Chapter 30, "Mission Demolition," but
these will be a bit more interesting. Take a moment to read the "Interpolation" section
of Appendix B, "Useful Concepts," before tackling the remaining enemies so that you
understand concepts like easing.
Enemy_2
Enemy_2 moves via a linear interpolation that is heavily eased by a sine wave. It rushes
in from the side of the screen, slows, reverses direction for a bit, slows, and then flies
off the screen in the original direction. This interpolation uses only two points, but the
u value will be drastically curved by a sine wave. The easing function for the u value of
Enemy_2 will be along the lines of:
u = u + 0.6 * Sin( 2π * u )
This is one of the easing functions explained in the "Interpolation" section of Appendix B.

Improving Enemy_2 with an AnimationCurve
The sine wave movement of Enemy_2 is pretty neat, but it would look a lot better with
some nice rotation. However, getting that rotation to match what we want with a math-
ematical formula (like we used for position) is going to be very difficult. In Figure 32.3a,
you can see the mathematical curve that we use for the linear interpolation of the ship
position, and Figure 32.3b shows a curve that I attempted to use to make the ship rotate
in a nice way…but it honestly looked pretty awful, with the ship wiggling a lot more than
I wanted. When you need more control over a curve than you can get with an equation,
an AnimationCurve is a great way to go. An AnimationCurve is a series of points on a
graph that allows you to control the conversion of one [0..1] value to another in much the
same way that we have been doing with our mathematical formulae, but the Animation-
Curve allows you to control it much more easily. I had some idea of the AnimationCurve
shape that I wanted from my experiments in defining a math-based curve (Figure 32.3b),
and I found that the Curve Editor window made it much easier to get the curve I wanted

6. Click Play to see the movement of these new enemies. Be sure to look at the lines
and curves that are being drawn in the Scene pane by each EnePyB 's call to
DraZDebug().
These lines and curves are an excellent example of what I call visual debugging. Game
development often involves a lot of information; too much to be easily represented by
text in a Console message. In total, each call to DraZDebug() draws 21 lines, illustrating
not only the three points controlling the curve and the shape of the curve itself but also
showing (through color) the direction of movement. Now, let's break down how it does
so by explaining comments // f – // i of Code Listing 32.10.
f. The Debug.DraZ/ine() method draws a temporary line in the Scene pane.
The first two parameters are the endpoints of the line, the third is the color,
and the last is the number of seconds the line should stay on screen before
disappearing. By setting the duration to lifeTiPe, we can draw the line once
and know that it will disappear at the same moment that the EnePyB finishes
its movement.
g. To draw the curve itself, we break it down into 19 individual lines. The 0
th
point
of the curve is stored in preYPoint.
h. The for loop starts at 1 (the point 1/20
th
(or 5%) of the way along the curve). It
calculates a 9ector pt that is 5% along the curve using 8tils.Be]ier() and
then chooses a &olor c that is 5% of the way from cyan to yellow.
i. Debug.DraZ/ine() draws a line from preYPoint to the current pt that will last
lifeTiPe. After this, pt is assigned to preYPoint so that the line will start in
the right place on the next iteration of the for loop.
I'm sure you can tell that I'm pretty excited about this visual debugging stuff. It has
made solving difficult code problems drastically easier on myriad occasions, and I have
never once regretted the time that I took to write some visual debugging code.
As you watch the movement of Enemy_3 GameObjects for a while, you'll notice a
couple things about the Bézier curve movement:
a. Even though the midpoint is far below the bottom of the screen, no Enemy_3
ever makes it all the way down to the bottom of the screen. This happens
because a Bézier curve touches both the start and end points but is only influ-
enced by the midpoint. So, each Enemy_3 will start off the top of the screen,
move down quickly, then slow and move back upward without ever touching
the bottom of the screen.
b. Enemy_3 slows down a lot in the middle of the curve. This is a feature (and
sometimes a curse) of the math that makes Bézier curves work. The individual
points of a Bézier curve are spaced further apart at the endpoints and much
closer together in the middle.

Shooting Revisited
The way that you learned to fire projectiles in the previous chapter was fine for a rough
prototype, but you need to add additional capabilities to get this game to the next level.
In this section, you will learn to build two different kinds of weapons with the ability to
expand that in the future. To enable this, you'll create a WeaponDefinition class that
allows you to define the behavior of each type of weapon.
The eWeaponType Enum
As described in Chapter 30, "Mission Demolition," an enum —short for enumeration—is
a way to associate various options together into a new kind of variable. In this game,
players will have the ability to switch and improve weapons by collecting power-ups
dropped by defeated enemies. This will also be a power-up that increases shield power.
To provide a single variable type to store all the possible kinds of power-ups, you will
create an enum called eWeaponType. I tend to start enum type names with a lowercase
" e " to help them stand out.
1. Right-click on the __ Scripts folder in the Project pane and choose Create > C# Script.
This creates a NewBehaviourScript in the __Scripts folder.
